uncited: *   **Input:** Volumetric scalar field data (regular grid), transfer function (TF), camera parameters (view/projection matrices), and rendering mode (transparent/solid).
*   **3D Texture:** Stores the entire volume in GPU memory.
*   **2D Texture Stack:** Stores slices as a stack of 2D textures.
*   Array of vertices defining planar polygons (quads or triangle fans) intersecting the volume bounding box.
*   For **View-Aligned**: Intersect slicing planes with the volume bounding box.
Sort resulting vertices in counter-clockwise order.
Uses fixed proxy geometry aligned with the principal axes (X, Y, Z) of the volume.
Requires storing the volume as three stacks of 2D textures (replicated data), consuming 3x memory.
Uses proxy geometry that is orthogonal to the viewing direction.
Requires 3D textures (or on-the-fly reconstruction from 2D stacks).
A variant of object-aligned rendering where data is stored as a set of 2D texture slices.
Proxy polygons are simple rectangles aligned with slices.
To avoid data replication, slices can be reconstructed on the fly, incurring performance overhead.
*   **Time Complexity:** Rendering time is proportional to the number of slices and the resolution of the image.
*   **3D Textures:** $O(N)$ where $N$ is the number of voxels.
*   **When to Use:** Interactive visualization where performance is critical and artifacts are acceptable or mitigated (e.g., view-aligned slices).
*   **When Not to Use:** High-quality offline rendering requiring precise sampling (use ray casting); memory-constrained environments with large volumes using 2D textures.
Texture-Based Volume Rendering was developed to accelerate volume rendering on graphics hardware.
